<p class="proj-lead">
The Black–Scholes formula looks like a closed box until you price the same option three different ways and watch them agree. This is a group paper and presentation on the Black–Scholes–Merton model: its derivation by hedging and by risk-neutral valuation, the Greeks, and how a delta-hedged trader earns or loses from them. The notebook that backs it up checks the numbers; my part was the hedging section, on the delta-neutral trader who is short gamma, and slides 15 to 17 with their formulas, code and plots.
</p>

## One price, three ways

A European call on a stock that pays no dividends, with spot 100 (110 for the in-the-money case), strike 100, 3% interest rate and 22% volatility. The first way is a Monte Carlo simulation of the stock at expiry. The second integrates the discounted payoff against the standard normal density. The third is the Black–Scholes formula itself, with the normal distribution function written through `erf`.

```python
def norm_cdf(x):
    return 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2)))

def black_scholes_call(S, K, T, r, sigma):
    d1 = (math.log(S / K) + (r + 0.5 * sigma**2) * T) / (sigma * math.sqrt(T))
    d2 = d1 - sigma * math.sqrt(T)
    return S * norm_cdf(d1) - K * math.exp(-r * T) * norm_cdf(d2)
```

| call                                 | closed form | Monte Carlo, 10,000 paths | error in standard errors |
| :----------------------------------- | ----------: | ------------------------: | -----------------------: |
| at the money, 30 days                |      2.6378 |             2.570 ± 0.038 |                     −1.8 |
| at the money, 120 days               |      5.5104 |             5.580 ± 0.083 |                     +0.8 |
| in the money ($$S = 110$$), 30 days  |     10.4187 |            10.491 ± 0.066 |                     +1.1 |
| in the money ($$S = 110$$), 120 days |     12.4702 |            12.633 ± 0.119 |                     +1.4 |

The numerical integration lands on the closed form to four decimals in every case (for example 2.63774 against 2.63775 for the at-the-money call at 30 days), which is what one expects, since it integrates the same expectation. The simulation lands within two standard errors of it in every case.

## The Greeks, by finite differences

The Greeks are the derivatives of the price. I estimated each by a central finite difference of the pricing function, which works even when no closed form exists, and checked them against the analytic expressions. For the at-the-money call with 30 days to expiry: delta 0.528, gamma 0.0631 per dollar, vega 0.114 per volatility point, theta −0.046 dollars per day (−16.9 a year) and rho 0.041 per percentage point of rate. The explorer below uses the analytic formulas; pick a Greek and compare expiries.

<div class="caption">Greeks of the call as a function of spot, for four expiries (strike 100, rate 3%, volatility 22%). Gamma and theta are largest at the money, and they sharpen as expiry approaches.</div>

## Where gamma meets theta

This is the part I wrote. A trader who has sold at-the-money options and hedges delta is short gamma: the position collects theta every day and pays for every move of the underlying through the gamma. For an at-the-money call with 30 days to expiry and 22% volatility, on 100,000 shares, theta brings in $4,631 a day, and the gamma loss cancels it when the spot moves to 98.79 or 101.23, about ±1.22%. The closed form is $$\pm\sigma/\sqrt{365}$$, here ±1.15% (98.85 and 101.15): I called it the Gamma–Theta Break-even Range, the GTBR. It is slightly narrower than the numerical break-even because it drops the interest-rate part of theta, and the 365 counts the days of the year because theta accrues daily.

<div class="caption">One-day P&L of the short-gamma, delta-hedged position: theta income, gamma loss and the total. The dashed lines are the closed-form GTBR; the dots are where the total crosses zero in this example.</div>

The derivation, the version in trading days ($$\sigma/\sqrt{252}$$, about 20% wider) and the question of whether the market tends to keep moving once it leaves the range are in a standalone follow-up: [GTBR: Gamma–Theta Break-even Range]({{ '/projects/9_gtbr/' | relative_url }}).
